blocks.text: When an MCP server starts struggling under load, there are two very different ways to respond.
You can make the one server bigger, or you can run more copies of it side by side.
This lesson is about the second option, horizontal scaling, and what makes it work well or badly.
1. Scaling Up vs Scaling Out

blocks.alt: One larger server instance is compared against a load balancer spreading traffic across many

blocks.text: Scaling up means giving your one MCP server instance more CPU, more memory, and hoping it copes.
Scaling out, also called horizontal scaling, means running more instances of that same server instead.
Both approaches add capacity, but they fail differently, and they cost differently as traffic keeps growing.

items: Scaling up hits a ceiling, eventually there is no bigger machine to move to.
Scaling up is an all or nothing move, one restart to resize means downtime.
Scaling out adds capacity in small increments, one instance at a time.
Scaling out survives a single instance crashing, the others keep serving traffic.

blocks.text: 2. What Horizontal Scaling Means for an MCP Server
For an MCP server, horizontal scaling means running several identical server processes at once.
Each instance registers the same tools, the same resources, and the same prompts as every other instance.
A client, or the host acting for it, should not be able to tell which instance actually answered a given request.
3. The Load Balancer in Front of Many Instances

blocks.alt: A load balancer sits in front of many server instances

blocks.text: Adding instances only helps if something spreads requests across them, that job belongs to a load balancer.
The load balancer sits between clients and the pool of MCP server instances, picking one instance per request.
A simple round robin policy is often enough, sending each new request to the next instance in turn.

blocks.title: The load balancer is not optional
blocks.content: Without something routing traffic across instances, adding more instances does nothing, requests still pile up on whichever one clients happen to reach directly.

blocks.text: 4. Autoscaling Based on Request Rate

blocks.alt: A rising request rate triggers autoscaling to add more instances

blocks.text: Autoscaling is the automated version of scaling out, adding or removing instances without a human watching a dashboard.
One common signal is request rate, how many tool calls or resource reads are arriving per second across the fleet.
When request rate climbs past a threshold, the autoscaler adds instances, and it removes them again once traffic drops.

code.content:
# autoscaling policy expressed as a simple config
metric: requests_per_second
target_per_instance: 50
min_instances: 2
max_instances: 20
scale_up_cooldown_seconds: 60
scale_down_cooldown_seconds: 300

blocks.text: 5. Autoscaling Based on CPU Usage
CPU usage is the other common signal, and it catches a different kind of pressure than request rate does.
A tool that runs a heavy computation can spike CPU on an instance even while request rate looks perfectly normal.
Most autoscalers let you combine signals, scaling up if either request rate or CPU usage crosses its own threshold.

blocks.text: 6. A Kubernetes HorizontalPodAutoscaler in Practice
If your MCP server instances run as pods in Kubernetes, the built in HorizontalPodAutoscaler does exactly this job.
You point it at a deployment, give it a target metric, and let it add or remove pods within a range you set.

code.content:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: mcp-server-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: mcp-server
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 65
    - type: Pods
      pods:
        metric:
          name: requests_per_second
        target:
          type: AverageValue
          averageValue: "50"

blocks.text: This one manifest tells Kubernetes to keep every pod near 65 percent CPU and around 50 requests per second.
Anywhere between 2 and 20 pods can exist at any moment, depending purely on real load.
7. Statelessness, the Property That Makes Scaling Easy

blocks.alt: Statelessness is compared against in memory state for how easy scaling is

blocks.text: None of this works cleanly unless your MCP server instances are stateless, meaning any instance can handle any request.
A stateless instance keeps nothing in memory that the next request depends on, it reads what it needs and writes what it needs, then forgets.
If every instance is interchangeable, the load balancer can send a request anywhere, and the autoscaler can add or remove instances freely.
That freedom is the whole point of horizontal scaling, and statelessness is what buys it.
8. In Memory State, the Property That Makes Scaling Hard
The opposite of statelessness is keeping important data in a single instance's memory, and only that instance knowing it.
Picture a server that tracks a conversation's history in a plain in-memory dictionary, keyed by session id.
The moment a second request for that same session lands on a different instance, that instance has no idea the conversation ever happened.

items: New instances added by the autoscaler start with empty memory, missing all existing session state.
Removing an instance during scale down silently deletes whatever state only it was holding.
The load balancer either has to pin a session to one instance, or state has to move somewhere shared.
Pinning sessions to one instance defeats much of the point of having a fleet at all.

blocks.text: 9. Connecting Back to Distributed MCP Architectures
This tension between statelessness and in memory state is exactly what the Distributed MCP Architectures lesson covers in depth.
That lesson walks through session affinity, shared caches, and shared databases as ways to handle state across a fleet.
Horizontal scaling and distributed architecture are really the same coin, one is the mechanism, the other is the state problem it forces you to solve.
10. Designing a Stateless MCP Server

blocks.alt: A stateless server design keeps no request specific state locally

blocks.text: Designing for statelessness starts with a simple habit, treat every incoming request as if it is the very first request that instance has ever seen.
Any data a tool needs beyond the current call should come from a database, a cache, or the request itself, never from local memory.

code.content:
# stateless tool handler, reads what it needs each call
async def get_forecast(city: str, session_id: str):
    session = await sessions_db.get(session_id)
    forecast = await weather_api.fetch(city)
    await sessions_db.append(session_id, {"tool": "get_forecast", "city": city})
    return forecast

blocks.text: Notice nothing here is stored on the instance itself, every instance running this exact function behaves identically.
11. Where Session State Should Live Instead

blocks.alt: Session state lives in a shared store instead of on any one instance

blocks.text: Once state moves out of instance memory, it has to live somewhere every instance can reach, usually a fast shared store.
The right choice depends on how long the data needs to survive and how quickly it needs to be read back.

blocks.text: 12. Testing That a Server Actually Scales
Adding an autoscaler is easy, trusting that it actually behaves as expected under real load is a different job entirely.
Testing scaling means generating real traffic, watching instance count change, and confirming response times stay healthy throughout.
It is not enough to read the autoscaler config and assume it works, you have to watch it happen.

items: Confirm new instances actually pass their readiness check before receiving traffic.
Confirm the load balancer starts sending requests to a new instance shortly after it joins.
Confirm response times recover once new instances come online, not just that instance count went up.
Confirm scale down does not drop requests that were mid flight on the removed instance.

blocks.text: 13. Load Testing an Autoscaling Deployment

blocks.alt: A load test drives traffic up to confirm autoscaling actually kicks in

blocks.text: A load test tool that ramps traffic up gradually is the most reliable way to watch autoscaling in action.
Ramping slowly lets you see the exact moment the autoscaler reacts, instead of overwhelming everything at once.

code.content:
# a simple ramping load test against an MCP server's HTTP endpoint
import asyncio, httpx, time

async def ramp(base_url, start_rps=5, step=5, step_seconds=30, max_rps=100):
    rps = start_rps
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        while rps <= max_rps:
            start = time.time()
            while time.time() - start < step_seconds:
                await client.post(f"{base_url}/tools/call", json={"name": "get_forecast"})
                await asyncio.sleep(1 / rps)
            print(f"ramped to {rps} requests per second")
            rps += step

blocks.text: While this runs, watch instance count, average response time, and error rate side by side on one dashboard.
Worked Example
A team runs an MCP server that answers product lookup tool calls for a shopping assistant.
The Starting Point
At launch they run two instances behind a load balancer, comfortably handling their normal daily traffic.
The Problem
During a flash sale, request rate jumps to ten times normal, and response times start climbing past two seconds.
Setting the Policy
They configure an autoscaler targeting 50 requests per second per instance, with a ceiling of 20 instances.
What Happens Under Load
As request rate climbs, the autoscaler adds instances every sixty seconds, going from 2 to 9 instances in under five minutes.
Response times drop back under 300 milliseconds within that same window, once enough instances are handling the load.
Verifying It Worked
The team replays this exact scenario in a staging environment using a ramping load test before trusting it in production.

items: Instance count in the dashboard matched what the policy predicted at each traffic level.
No request during the ramp returned an error or timed out.
Scale down after the sale ended happened gradually, not all at once.

blocks.text: Common Mistakes
A few mistakes show up again and again when teams first set up horizontal scaling for MCP servers.

items: Keeping session data in instance memory, then wondering why new instances lose context.
Setting the max instance limit too low, so the autoscaler hits a ceiling right when it is needed most.
Never actually load testing, and finding out the policy is wrong during a real traffic spike.
Ignoring scale down cooldowns, causing instances to flap up and down on noisy metrics.
Forgetting readiness checks, so the load balancer sends traffic to instances that are not ready yet.

blocks.text: Practice
Try these to make horizontal scaling concrete rather than theoretical.

items: Take an MCP server you have written and find any place it stores data in a local variable across calls.
Write a Kubernetes HorizontalPodAutoscaler manifest for that server, choosing sensible min and max replicas.
Write a small ramping load test script and run it against a local deployment with two instances.
Watch what happens to response times before and after a third instance joins the pool.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway
Horizontal scaling adds capacity by running more instances, not by growing one instance bigger.
Statelessness is what makes that possible, and testing under real load is what proves it actually works.
